units.text: Quba: Waiting, Arrival, and the Road to Madinah
How did those waiting recognize the Prophet ﷺ among the arrivals at Quba, with whom did he stay, and how long was his stay according to the accounts?
From the people waiting at the edge of the lava plain to recognizing the Prophet ﷺ among the arrivals and his stay with Banu Amr ibn Awf, Quba opens the way to Madinah.
Days of waiting, a moment of recognition

The Muslims went out to the lava plain to await the arrival from Makkah until the midday heat drove them back to their homes. Then a Jewish man spotted the party and called out, and the people went out to meet them. In Ibn Ishaq’s account, men of the Ansar describe waiting after the dawn prayer, then returning indoors before they heard the man’s call.

The party headed to Banu Amr ibn Awf. Abu Bakr stood before the people while the Prophet ﷺ sat silently; some of the arriving Ansar who had not seen him greeted Abu Bakr at first. When the sun fell on the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr shaded him with his cloak, and they recognized him. The men describing the reception in Ibn Ishaq’s account likewise tell of recognition when the shade receded.
In the homes of Quba

Ibn Ishaq then mentions that the Prophet ﷺ lodged with Kulthum ibn Hidm, according to what some relate, and cites another view that he stayed with Sad ibn Khaythama. Those who name Kulthum explain that the Prophet would sit with people in Sad’s house, known as the house of the unmarried men. Ibn Ishaq leaves the two accounts without deciding the host’s name.

As for Abu Bakr, Ibn Ishaq places his lodging with Khubayb ibn Isaf, and also cites another view naming Kharija ibn Zayd. The account of his lodging remains distinct from the account of the Prophet’s ﷺ lodging.
Days at Quba

In Ibn Ishaq’s account, the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Quba on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday and left on Friday; nevertheless, he mentions the claim of Banu Amr ibn Awf that he remained with them longer. Urwa describes the stay in al-Bukhari’s account as several nights beyond ten, while Anas, in al-Bayhaqi’s report, specifies fourteen nights.
A mosque at Quba

Ibn Ishaq mentions the Prophet ﷺ founding his mosque at Quba as part of the account of his stay, while Urwa mentions founding the mosque and praying in it. Those staying there had a place to pray in Quba before the party proceeded to Madinah; the account of the mosque does not depend on selecting a single number of nights for the stay.

After the move into Madinah, Urwa’s account describes the site of the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque as a date-drying yard belonging to Suhayl and Sahl, and recounts his bargaining with them for it. In Anas’s account, the Prophet ﷺ asks Banu al-Najjar for the price of their walled plot and they reply; Anas then continues the account of construction in the next part of the excerpt. Each description belongs to its own report; this is not the construction of the Quba mosque.
Toward Friday on the road

The Prophet ﷺ left Quba; in Ibn Ishaq’s account, Friday came upon him among Banu Salim ibn Awf, and he prayed the Friday prayer in the mosque of the valley. In Urwa’s account, the riding animal continues until it kneels at the site of the mosque in Madinah. From here begin the accounts of the stay in Madinah, after the days at Quba and its mosque.
Which day, and how long?

Ibn Hajar cites reports placing it at the beginning of Rabi al-Awwal or varying numbers of days later, then proposes ways to reconcile them, including differences in sighting the new moon. Elsewhere he suggests that some who gave a shorter duration may not have counted the day of arrival or departure.

Elsewhere Ibn Hajar lists stays of three, five, fourteen, and twenty-two days, and says Anas’s report is more deserving of acceptance: that is his preference among reports in that passage. When discussing variant wordings of one particular transmission, however, he says al-Mustamli and al-Hamawi have twenty-four while the others have fourteen, calling the latter correct specifically for this line of transmission. Judging the wording of a version here is not the same as the broader comparison there.
Identifying the mosque founded on God-consciousness

Ibn Hajar quotes the verse and the majority view applying it to Quba, then relates a reported prophetic answer identifying the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque, and another report mentioning Quba’s merit alongside that identification.

Ibn Hajar cites al-Qurtubi’s explanation of why the answer might single out the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque, then offers another possibility of his own and says both mosques were founded on God-consciousness. Ibn Hajar also cites from Abu Dawud Abu Hurayra’s report from the Prophet ﷺ that the Quran verse about men who love to purify themselves was revealed concerning the people of Quba. Ibn Hajar explains that the answer identifying the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque dispels the idea that founding on God-consciousness belongs to the Quba mosque alone; he also relates al-Dawudi’s and al-Suhayli’s view that both mosques were founded on God-consciousness.

They would go out every morning to the lava plain and wait for him until the midday heat drove them back. One day, after waiting a long time, they returned; when they had reached their houses, a Jewish man climbed one of their fortified buildings to look at something and saw the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions, dressed in white, shimmering in the mirage. The Jewish man could not help crying at the top of his voice: “People of the Arabs! Here is your good fortune for which you have been waiting!” The Muslims sprang to their weapons and met the Messenger of God ﷺ on the upper stretch of the lava plain. He turned with them to the right until he stopped among Banu Amr ibn Awf. This was on a Monday in the month of Rabi al-Awwal. Abu Bakr stood facing the people while the Messenger of God ﷺ sat silent. The Ansar who came and had not seen the Messenger of God ﷺ began greeting Abu Bakr, until the sun fell on the Messenger of God ﷺ. Abu Bakr came over and shaded him with his cloak, and then the people recognized the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Messenger of God ﷺ remained among Banu Amr ibn Awf for some ten-plus nights. The mosque founded on God-consciousness was founded, and the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed in it. Then he mounted his riding animal and traveled with the people walking beside him until it knelt at the Messenger’s ﷺ mosque in Madinah. At that time some Muslim men were praying there; it was a yard for drying dates belonging to Suhayl and Sahl, two orphan boys in the care of Asad ibn Zurara.

“When we heard that the Messenger of God ﷺ had departed from Makkah and were awaiting [1] his arrival, we would go out after the dawn prayer to the outer edge of our lava plain to wait for the Messenger of God ﷺ. By God, we would not leave until the sun overcame the shaded places; when we could find no shade, we went indoors. These were hot days. On the day the Messenger of God ﷺ arrived, we sat as usual until there was no shade left, then went into our houses. The Messenger of God ﷺ arrived as we went indoors. The first to see him was a Jewish man who had seen what we had been doing and knew that we awaited the Messenger of God’s ﷺ arrival among us. He shouted at the top of his voice, ‘O Banu Qayla [2], your good fortune has arrived!’ He said: We went out to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who was in the shade of a palm tree with Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, who was of a similar age. Most of us had not seen the Messenger of God ﷺ before. People crowded around him [3] without distinguishing him from Abu Bakr, until the shade moved away from the Messenger of God ﷺ. Abu Bakr stood and shaded him with his cloak, and then we recognized him [4].”

Ibn Ishaq said: The Messenger of God ﷺ lodged, as they relate, with Kulthum [1] ibn Hidm, of Banu Amr ibn Awf and, more specifically, Banu Ubayd. It is also said: Rather, he lodged with Sad ibn Khaythama. Those who say that he lodged with Kulthum ibn Hidm say that when the Messenger of God ﷺ left Kulthum’s house, he would sit with people in Sad ibn Khaythama’s house. This was because Sad was unmarried and had no family, and his home was the lodging of the unmarried men [2] among the Messenger of God’s ﷺ emigrant Companions. Hence the saying that he lodged with Sad ibn Khaythama. Sad ibn Khaythama’s house was called “the house of the unmarried men.” God knows best which it was; we have heard both.

His words, “And that was on a Monday in the month of Rabi al-Awwal”: this is the accepted account; the person who said Friday held an anomalous view. In Musa ibn Uqba’s report from Ibn Shihab, he arrived there at the new moon of Rabi al-Awwal, that is, on its first day. In Jarir ibn Hazim’s report from Ibn Ishaq, he arrived there when two nights of Rabi al-Awwal had passed; Abu Mashar gives something similar, but says it was Monday night. Something similar comes from Ibn al-Barqi, and likewise appears toward the end of Sahih Muslim. In Ibrahim ibn Sad’s report from Ibn Ishaq, he arrived there when twelve nights of Rabi al-Awwal had passed. Abu Said, in Sharaf al-Mustafa by way of Abu Bakr ibn Hazm, has his arrival on the thirteenth of Rabi al-Awwal. This and the preceding account can be reconciled by differences in sighting the new moon. He also reports from Umar that he then lodged among Banu Amr ibn Awf on Monday with two nights of Rabi al-Awwal remaining: that is how it reads. Perhaps it originally said “two nights had passed,” agreeing with the report of Jarir ibn Hazim. Al-Zubayr in Khabar al-Madina reports from Ibn Shihab that it was the middle of Rabi al-Awwal. It is also said his arrival was on the seventh. Ibn Hazm states categorically that he left Makkah with three nights of Safar remaining; this agrees with Hisham ibn al-Kalbi’s statement that he left the cave on Monday night, the first day of Rabi al-Awwal. If that is accurately preserved, perhaps his arrival at Quba was Monday the eighth of Rabi al-Awwal. Coupled with Anas’s statement that he stayed at Quba fourteen nights, this would mean that he entered Madinah on the twenty-second of that month. But al-Kalbi states categorically that he entered it after twelve nights of the month had passed; according to his statement, his stay at Quba would have been only four nights. Ibn Hibban also states this categorically, saying that he stayed there Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday—that is, left on Friday—as though he did not count the day of departure. Similarly Musa ibn Uqba says he stayed with them three nights, as though he counted neither the departure nor the arrival day. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar relates from some of Banu Amr ibn Awf that he stayed among them twenty-two days. Something close to it occurs in Urwa ibn al-Zubayr’s mursal report, as will be mentioned next. Most reports say he arrived in daylight, while Muslim’s report says at night. They can be reconciled by saying the arrival was at the end of the night and the entry was by day.

His words, “The Messenger of God ﷺ remained among Banu Amr ibn Awf for some ten-plus nights”: in the report of Anas in the next chapter, he stayed with them fourteen nights. I have mentioned above reports that differ; God knows best. Musa ibn Uqba said, from Ibn Shihab: he stayed with them three days. He said: Ibn Shihab also transmitted from Mujammi ibn Haritha that he stayed twenty-two nights. Ibn Ishaq said: he stayed with them five days, while Banu Amr ibn Awf claim it was longer. I say: Anas was not of Banu Amr ibn Awf, for they belonged to the Aws while Anas belonged to the Khazraj. He stated definitively what I have cited, so his account is more deserving of acceptance than the others.

It was the first mosque built—that is, in Madinah.
